title: The spoon and the soup (64–68)
hook: a fool beside a wise person all his life knows the truth no more than a spoon tastes the soup

segments.voice: Yesterday, bala: the fool who knows he's a fool is wise at least that far. Your line: wise so far.

A ladle sits in a pot of soup at a family dinner. It's been in there for hours. It has stirred the onions, the broth, the spices, touched every drop. It's been closer to that soup than anyone at the table, and it has tasted absolutely nothing. Then a guest walks in, takes one spoonful off the ladle, and knows the whole soup in a second. The Dhammapada puts those two side by side, and asks what makes the difference.
screen: `A LADLE IN THE POT FOR HOURS.` → `IT HAS TASTED NOTHING.` → `ONE SIP, AND THE GUEST KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-four, in Müller's English: “If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.” And its twin, verse sixty-five: “If an intelligent man be associated for one minute only with a wise man, he will soon perceive the truth, as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.” A lifetime next to wisdom, or one minute. The difference isn't how close you are. It's whether you taste. The commentary tells verse sixty-four about an elder named Udayi who liked to sit in the teacher's seat. Visiting monks assumed he must be learned and asked him questions, and he couldn't answer a single one. Years near the teaching, like the ladle. Verse sixty-five goes with a lively story from the monastic rulebook: thirty young men out for a day in the woods with their wives, one of them with a hired companion, who ran off with their things. Chasing her, they met the Buddha sitting under a tree and asked if he'd seen a woman go by. He asked them: which is better, to go looking for a woman, or to go looking for yourselves? They sat down to listen. In one conversation, the story says, they understood, and asked to become monks. Verses sixty-six to sixty-eight add a practical test: a deed is well done when you don't regret it afterward, when you remember it with gladness. So this isn't about being near good things. It's about letting them in.
screen: `A LIFETIME, LIKE A SPOON.` · `ONE MINUTE, LIKE A TONGUE.` · `UDAYI IN THE TEACHER'S SEAT.` · `LOOKING FOR YOURSELVES.` · then, large: `TASTE THE SOUP.`

segments.voice: Take one breath and taste it: the cool at the nostrils, the rise of the chest, the small pause at the top, the long release. All day the breath has gone on unnoticed, like a ladle stirring the pot. For a couple of minutes, be the tongue: not thinking about breathing, just tasting each one.
Dabbi. A spoon, or ladle: one in the soup all its life tastes nothing, while a tongue tastes it in a moment.
Your line: taste the soup. The spoon is near; the tongue tastes. That's day one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the spoon-and-soup verses to stress that being near teachers or temples is not the same as taking the teaching in, and to encourage wholehearted listening.

original.note: Pali: spoon or ladle, from verse sixty-four: 'dabbi suparasam yatha,' as a spoon the taste of soup.

trapdoor: what you thought: the spoon verse is an insult to people who aren't clever.
what it means: nearness isn't enough; you have to taste. anyone can be the spoon or the tongue.
what a scholar hears: the thirty young men (the Bhaddavaggiya) come from the Vinaya's Mahavagga I; the commentary attaches their story to verse 65.
